topics.title: SOLID Quick Reference Matrix
topics.definition: A 1-page condensed review cheat sheet of the 5 SOLID design principles with violation symptoms and immediate modern C++ refactoring remedies.
topics.why_it_matters: Perfect for a 5-minute review right before entering an interview waiting room.
topics.real_world_analogy: A laminated emergency checklist in an airplane cockpit.
conceptual_breakdown: S - Single Responsibility: 1 class = 1 responsibility.
O - Open/Closed: Open for extension, closed for modification.
L - Liskov Substitution: Subtypes must be substitutable for base types.
I - Interface Segregation: Client-specific narrow interfaces.
D - Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions, not concretes.

steps.description: Is a class modifying 5 unrelated features? -> Fix SRP.
Are you adding case statements for new types? -> Fix OCP with Strategy/Factory.
Are clients implementing empty dummy methods? -> Fix ISP by splitting interfaces.

step_by_step_explanation: 2. Add SMS or Slack senders without modifying UserNotifier: (OCP).

common_mistakes.mistake: Over-engineering tiny scripts into 20 SOLID classes
common_mistakes.correction: Apply SOLID where requirements evolve, vary, or grow complex.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Can SOLID principles conflict with performance?'
Answer: Virtual function indirection in deep OOP hierarchies can incur cache misses. In latency-critical hot paths, templates / CRTP (static polymorphism) achieve SOLID decoupling with zero runtime overhead.

topics.title: Design Pattern Selection Decision Tree
topics.definition: A visual and conceptual decision tree mapping any system design problem directly to the optimal GoF design pattern.
topics.why_it_matters: Eliminates hesitation during interview pattern selection.
topics.real_world_analogy: A medical diagnostic flowchart for fast triage.
conceptual_breakdown: Object Creation? $\to$ Factory (variants), Builder (step-by-step), Prototype (clone), Singleton (1 instance).
Interface Incompatibility? $\to$ Adapter (convert), Facade (simplify), Bridge (decouple abstraction from implementation).
Adding Behavior? $\to$ Decorator (wrap), Proxy (access control), Composite (tree structures).
Varying Algorithms or State? $\to$ Strategy (algorithm), State (lifecycle), Observer (events), Command (undo/redo).

steps.description: Need to construct an object with 10 optional parameters? -> BUILDER.
Need to notify multiple subscribers of data changes? -> OBSERVER.
Need to execute, queue, or undo user actions? -> COMMAND.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Identify the Primary Intent: Is the problem about creation, structure, or behavior?
2. Match with Decision Tree: Pick the minimal pattern that solves the extensibility requirement.
3. Avoid Overuse: If a plain function or enum suffices, do not introduce a complex pattern.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using Abstract Factory when a simple Factory Method suffices
common_mistakes.correction: Abstract Factory is only needed when creating *families* of related products.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why not use Builder for everything instead of constructors?'
Answer: Builder introduces boilerplate. For simple structs with 2-3 fields, standard constructors or C++20 designated initializers (`Point{.x=1, .y=2}`) are simpler and faster.

topics.title: UML Relationships & C++ Code Mappings
topics.definition: Visual cheat sheet mapping every UML arrow symbol (Dependency, Association, Aggregation, Composition, Generalization, Realization) to exact C++20 pointer and reference code.
topics.why_it_matters: Instantly eliminates confusion when drawing class diagrams on whiteboards.
topics.real_world_analogy: A translator dictionary converting English words directly into French phrases.
conceptual_breakdown: Dependency ($-\-\succ$): Function parameter or local variable (Uses).
Association ($-$): Member pointer or reference (Has-a).
Aggregation ($\diamond-$): Shared ownership (std::shared_ptr).
Composition ($\blacklozenge-$): Exclusive ownership (std::unique_ptr or direct value).
Generalization ($\triangle-$): Class inheritance (`public Base`).
Realization ($-\-\triangle$): Interface implementation (`public IInterface`).

steps.description: UML: Filled Diamond (Composition) -> C++: std::unique_ptr<Engine> or direct value member.
UML: Dashed Arrow (Dependency) -> C++: void process(const Context& ctx).

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Composition: Value types or std::unique_ptr enforce that child dies when parent dies.
2. Aggregation: std::shared_ptr or std::weak_ptr allow child to survive parent.
3. Dependency: Passing via parameter prevents persistent coupling.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing Composition when Aggregation is intended
common_mistakes.correction: If an Employee can switch Departments without being deleted from existence, Department -> Employee is Aggregation, NOT Composition.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why should we prefer Composition over Inheritance in UML?'
Answer: Composition provides loose coupling, dynamic runtime swapping of behavior, avoids fragile base class hierarchies, and adheres to the Open-Closed Principle.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Convert a rigid inheritance hierarchy into a flexible composition relationship.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: class Car : public V8Engine { ... }; // Inheritance anti-pattern
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: class Car { private: unique_ptr<IEngine> engine; }; // Clean Composition

practice_problem.title: Map UML Symbols to C++ Code

practice_problem.hint: University to Department (Composition), Department to Professor (Aggregation).

topics.title: Smart Pointers Ownership Cheat Sheet
topics.definition: Fast-reference guide for modern C++ smart pointer ownership semantics: `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, `weak_ptr`, and custom deleters.
topics.why_it_matters: Clean memory ownership is the bedrock of modern C++ LLD.
topics.real_world_analogy: Vehicle ownership titles: 1 sole owner (`unique_ptr`), co-signers on a joint lease (`shared_ptr`), or a parking attendant with temporary inspection access (`weak_ptr`).
conceptual_breakdown: std::unique_ptr: Exclusive ownership (Zero memory/CPU overhead compared to raw pointer).
std::shared_ptr: Shared ownership via reference-counted control block (16 bytes: ptr + ctrl block).
std::weak_ptr: Non-owning observer preventing circular reference memory leaks.
make_unique / make_shared: Exception-safe single memory allocation.

steps.description: std::make_shared allocates ManagedObject and ControlBlock in 1 contiguous memory block.
Copying shared_ptr increments strongCount to 2 with atomic increment.
weak_ptr observes object without incrementing strongCount.
Both shared_ptrs go out of scope -> strongCount = 0 -> Object destructor runs.

step_by_step_explanation: 2. Lockable Weak Pointers: wPtr.lock() returns a valid shared_ptr if alive or nullptr if destroyed.
3. Break Cycles: Always use weak_ptr for parent pointers or observer lists.

common_mistakes.mistake: Creating two independent `std::shared_ptr` from the same raw pointer
common_mistakes.correction: Creates two separate control blocks leading to double deletion crash. Always use `std::make_shared`.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why does std::make_shared keep control block memory allocated if weak_ptr is still alive after object destruction?'
Answer: `make_shared` allocates object and control block contiguously; the object is destructed when `strongCount == 0`, but the single memory buffer cannot be freed until `weakCount == 0`.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Fix a double-free bug caused by multiple shared_ptr creations from raw pointer.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: Resource* r = new Resource(); shared_ptr<Resource> p1(r); shared_ptr<Resource> p2(r);
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: auto p1 = std::make_shared<Resource>(); auto p2 = p1;

topics.title: C++ Concurrency & Thread Safety Rules
topics.definition: A 1-page condensed reference of C++ concurrency primitives: `std::mutex`, `std::shared_mutex`, `std::atomic`, memory orders, and condition variable idioms.
topics.why_it_matters: Essential reference for writing bug-free concurrent systems in LLD interviews.
topics.real_world_analogy: Safety checklist for high-voltage power stations: grounding rods, insulated gloves, and lock-out/tag-out switches.
conceptual_breakdown: Rule 1: Always lock with RAII (`std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_lock`, `std::scoped_lock`).
Rule 2: Always check condition variable predicate in a `while` loop (or use lambda predicate) to handle Spurious Wakeups.
Rule 3: Use `std::shared_mutex` for high read-to-write ratios.
Rule 4: Default to `std::memory_order_seq_cst` unless profiling proves atomic bottleneck.
Rule 5: Use `alignas(64)` on atomics accessed by separate threads to eliminate False Sharing.

steps.description: OS delivers Spurious Wakeup with queue still empty.
Predicate evaluates false -> Thread automatically goes back to sleep!

step_by_step_explanation: 1. RAII Locks: std::lock_guard in push, std::unique_lock in pop.
2. Spurious Wakeup Protection: cv.wait with lambda predicate automatically loops until !q.empty() is true.
3. Move Semantics: std::move() transfers elements without costly copies.

rows: Fast (Futex in user space if uncontended)

common_mistakes.mistake: Using `cv.wait(lock)` without checking a predicate in a loop
common_mistakes.correction: Spurious wakeups from the OS kernel can wake the thread while the queue is still empty, causing segfaults.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why does cv.wait require std::unique_lock instead of std::lock_guard?'
Answer: `cv.wait()` must be able to atomically release the mutex when entering sleep and re-acquire it upon waking up. `std::lock_guard` cannot be unlocked and re-locked.
